items.html:
All regular road generation 3 coverage in Ghana was made with a unique Google car. It has a visible roof rack with a piece of black tape on the right end of the front bar. In addition, the hood of the car is usually visible, showing a street view car wrapping that features a red rectangle and some other recognizable elements. Normally, this unique car is all you need to identify Ghana.

NOTE: Several natural reserves were covered with different unique cars.
Generation 4 coverage in Ghana was taken using a grey or white pickup truck with an antenna in the front. The truck will be either fully or partially blurred most of the time.

Ghana uses white plates on normal vehicles, and yellow plates for commercial vehicles. They can be long or short. Because commercial vehicles are really common, you will often see a mix of both plate colours.

NOTE: Nigeria has similar white plates, but a green tint should be visible, which helps differentiate them.
Ghana is mostly flat with red soil, however hills and mountains can be seen in some regions. Tropical vegetation is very common, and palms are common especially toward the south.
Taxis in Ghana typically have multicoloured body panels. The fenders and quarter panels are always coloured orange-yellow.
Road lines in Ghana are always white. However, many paved roads do not have road lines at all.

Ghana typically uses wooden poles with 3 insulators on a metallic crossbar.

NOTE: Kenya has a similar pole.
Ghana is a patriotic country, and you can often see things painted in the national flag’s colours: red, yellow, green, and sometimes including the black star.

Black and white striped signposts in Ghana are typically seen in cities. On rural roads, you will mostly see classic, non-painted, metal signposts.

NOTE: Black and white signposts can be seen in other countries as well. Make sure to look at other clues before guessing.

The coverage in Ghana is limited and easy to memorize, as most of it was taken on its main roads and in major cities. The most dense coverage is located in the south, around the cities of Accra and Kumasi.
The majority of generation 4 coverage is close to Accra or Kumasi, with only a few major roads being covered.

This map shows the distribution of paved and unpaved roads across the country.

_You can click on the image to enlarge it._

Ghana features 3 distinct types of tape on the google car:

In the southwest, you can find the ‘unpeeled tape’, which is essentially a mostly intact tape, which is not peeling off.

In the east and north, you can find the ‘peeled tape’, which unlike the ‘unpeeled tape’, is slightly peeled off.

North of Kumasi, and west of Tamale, you can find this ‘scotched tape’, which has two distinct white spots on the left side of the tape.
Northern Ghana features a savannah landscape, which can be identified by its dry soil and less dense vegetation.

Tall mountain ranges in Ghana are typically seen near Lake Volta in the highlighted area.

NOTE: Mountain ranges to the east are more common in the area near Togo.
Dense forests in Ghana are typically found in the southwest and east. You will usually see many naturally occurring palm trees, making the two regions recognizable.
Tall palm trees are commonly found along the coast. Most of them are located in the west.

Most unpaved roads in a dry savannah landscape are found north of Wa, as well as near the town itself.

NOTE: The other unpaved roads in northern Ghana are the Yendi-Nkwanta road in the east, and part of the Salaga-Tamale road, which has very distinct soil. See the tips below.

The road connecting the town of Sawla with the N10 has very crisp, new road lines. Most of the road runs in a general east-west direction, through a lush savannah landscape. The middle line can be solid or dashed.

NOTE: There are a couple of other roads with crisp road lines like these, however these tend to have a different road angle or landscape.

The Salaga-Tamale road up to Kpalbusi is a dirt road with very moody overcast coverage. The soil tends to be very dark, with a purple or brown tinge to it. The road also has a unique tropical savannah feel. The soil is most dark near the town of Salaga.

NOTE: Unpaved roads with overcast coverage and a savannah landscape can be found in other places. The unique aspect of this road is the dark purplish brown soil and the especially dark cloud cover.

The road between Nkwanta and Domanko is unpaved, with a powerline close to the road to your east or northeast. The road itself runs in a general SE-NW direction, through a lush savannah landscape that is typical of central Ghana.

NOTE: In urban areas, there can be a powerline on both sides of the road. In addition, a section of the Salaga-Tamale road has a powerline to the east as well, but the darker soil and moody cloud cover makes it distinguishable.

On a section of the N2 east of Lake Volta, you can often see a ridgeline to your southeast, somewhat close to the road. The road itself also has a distinct angle, running in a general SW-NE direction. The sky is very overcast and grey.

The coastal area just east of Accra, especially on the N1, has a distinct landscape: it is very flat and wide open, with significantly less vegetation than the rest of southern Ghana. Some parts can look somewhat dry.

The section of the N1 road near the border town of Elubo is very new: it has dark and unblemished asphalt, a very crisp-looking middle line, and no outer lines. The vegetation is dense and occasionally features palm trees.

NOTE: This new road surface continues until the town of Azuleti. The middle line can be dashed or solid. Near Azuleti, the road does not have a middle line.

The Keta Lagoon in the southeast of Ghana can be seen on the road that runs along it, with the lake being most visible in the northern section. You can sometimes see grey rocks on the side of the road. The soil is quite sandy in comparison to the rest of the country, and it should have a coastal feel.
Several nature reserves and sanctuaries have this unique car. A white car and side mirrors will be visible instead of the regular car, however, the ‘Ghana tape’ will still be there.

The Ankasa Game Reserve has a unique Google car. The entire front of the Google car can be seen, with only the actual camera blurred. The roof of the car will have a street view vinyl and the ‘Ghana tape’ will be present.

The Boabeng Fiema Monkey Sanctuary has a unique Google car. The ‘Ghana tape’ and roof rack will not be visible however, the black right side mirror will be slightly visible just outside the blur.

NOTE: The red soil and surrounding vegetation should still be good clues for the country, despite the lack of the typical car meta associated with Ghana.

lm.name: "KP" Consonant Cluster
lm.note: "KP" next to each other can be seen much more commonly in the Greater Accra and Volta provinces due to local language influence. Credits to seb010101 for this meta, which was posted in Lupus' Regionguessing Meta Library.

lm.name: Accra Antenna
lm.note: Having an antenna in Ghana is extremely rare, but when it is there, it only appears in Accra.

lm.name: Accra Houses
lm.note: Kind of a fake meta, but as a rule of thumb, most residential buildings in Accra look like this (light beige walls and triangle sheet metal roof) and almost none do in Kumasi, with about half of them looking like this in other major cities.

lm.name: Asokwa Leaf
lm.note: This leaf above the tape appears north of Asokwa and on either side of Obuasi. Credits to amordys for showing me this meta, and thibeauvanuden for giving a more accurate distribution and making the attached image (which was published on Lupus' Regionguessing Meta Library).

lm.name: Bar Ring
lm.note: A small ring in one of the roof racks of the car can be found in the general southwest of the country. Credits to thibeauvanuden for this meta, which was shared in Lupus' Regionguessing Meta Library.

lm.name: Bimbila-Nkwanta Road
lm.note: The road going from Bimbila to Nkwanta has wooden poles to the northeast, and looks very dry but green. It is also unpaved.

lm.name: Boabeng Car
lm.note: Most features of the car are missing in Boabeng and its reserve, which are disconnected from the rest of the coverage. The right mirror is still there though.

lm.name: Bui Natpark Road
lm.note: The road to the east of Bui National Park has grainy pavement and is driving north or northwest.

lm.name: Cape Coast Street Signs
lm.note: Street signs in Cape Coast are always green, say "CCMA" on them, and will show up at most intersections. Street signs in Kumasi will rarely also be green - they don't say "CCMA" but may be hard to distinguish from farther away.

lm.name: Coastal Cape Coast Road
lm.note: This road in Cape Coast is the only somewhat rural coastal road driving east.

lm.name: Ho Hills
lm.note: The town of Ho has prominent hills to the northwest.

lm.name: Huni Valley Road
lm.note: This road near Huni Valley is unpaved and surrounded by palm trees and short palm-looking shrubs. It can drive any direction except south, but is usually driving north.

lm.name: Juaso-Nsawam Road
lm.note: The road from Nsawam to Juaso drives north or northwest, and is either badly paved or a dirt road. Travelling from Nsawam to New Abirem, the road shows increasingly worse condition before improving again as you get closer to Juaso.

lm.name: Keta
lm.note: Keta is a town next to an inland lake - the lake will usually not be visible, but everything will feel very coastal with palm trees while also feeling quite dry and sandy at most parts.

lm.name: Keta Lagoon
lm.note: The road in Keta Lagoon Protected Area drives southeast, is taken close to sunset, and most importantly looks very dry but still very green.

lm.name: Koforidua Hills
lm.note: The city of Koforidua has prominent hills to the northeast.

lm.name: Kumasi Street Signs
lm.note: Kumasi can have several different colored street signs, which correspond to what part of the city you're in. Credits to torgeantihl for finding this meta and creating the image, which was published in Lupus' Regionguessing Meta Library.

lm.name: Max West N1
lm.note: The westernmost part of the N1 looks very clean and freshly paved, and can either have no road lines or only center road lines.

lm.name: Mole Natpark Road
lm.note: The road in Mole National Park (which continues and keeps its appearance from Sawla to Fulfoso) has very grainy pavement, drives east (except a small south-driving section), and has deep orange soil on either side of the road.

lm.name: N2 Rifts
lm.note: Only the section of the N2 in the Oti and Northern regions will have rifts, while the sections in Volta and Greater Accra will not. (I didn't check rifts on every road, because some are so subtle that it feels like I'm making stuff up, so only use this to regionguess the road if you know you're on it)

lm.name: Normal Car
lm.note: This is the car you will normally see in Ghana, which can be found nearly everywhere but less common in Ashanti and nearby provinces (the region Kumasi is in). This low quality image is the only one I have and I lost the json, but blue is the normal car (which can also be mostly blurred but always has a crisp edge).

lm.name: Peeled Tape
lm.note: Peeled tape is more common in the north and east of the country. (Image from the Plonk It guide)

lm.name: Phone Codes
lm.note: Ghanaian phone codes follow a general south-to-north pattern. Around 1/3 of the phone codes you see are actually useful - phone codes starting with 02 or 05 can be anywhere.

lm.name: Region Names
lm.note: Ghanaian region names appear on many signs, and are especially useful for moving but have helped me before on NM and even NMPZ too.

lm.name: Salaga Road
lm.note: The road driving from Tamale to Salaga is perhaps the most recognizable in the entire country - it is very overcast and has extremely dark soil, which becomes darker the closer you get to Salaga.

lm.name: Spotted Tape
lm.note: Tape with two white spots on it can be found northwest of Kumasi and around Mole National Park.

lm.name: Sri Car
lm.note: A car with a French flag on the front resembling Sri Lanka's Google car can be found in the general southwest of the country. This low quality picture is all I have and I lost the JSON, but red is Sri car (which can also include a fully blurred front).

lm.name: Street Signs
lm.note: Blue street signs are most common in Accra, where they appear at nearly every intersection. However, blue street signs can also rarely appear in Kumasi or other towns. (There will also usually be a blue sticker on the poles for street signs in Accra - credits to seb010101 for this meta, which was published in Lupus' Regionguessing Meta Library.)

lm.name: Tamale-Navrongo Road
lm.note: The road going from Tamale to Navrongo is very dry with only shrubs on either side of the road. This can be distinguished from other dry roads because the car is driving north (or west for one small section) and a handful of clouds are scattered throughout the sky.

lm.name: Techiman Street Signs
lm.note: Street signs in Techiman are very common and always black. Black street signs can also rarely appear in Kumasi, however.

lm.name: Unpeeled Tape
lm.note: Unpeeled tape is most common in the general south of the country.

lm.name: Wa Road
lm.note: This road goes north from Wa and circles back to meet it in the northeast of the city. It can easily be regionguessed by driving direction, which goes clockwise. It becomes unpaved around 1/4 of the way through, and can be distinguished from other dry roads because it has much oranger soil (and also either very wispy clouds or none at all, if you'd rather play the game that way).

lm.name: West Coast Road
lm.note: This road on the west coast of Ghana is the only west-driving, rural, coastal road.

lm.name: Yendi-Bimbila Road
lm.note: The road from Yendi to Bimbila is unpaved and very dry, with orange soil. It looks almost identical to south-driving parts of the Wa road but has more scattered clouds in the distance.

lm.name: Ghana
lm.note:
Format 03X XXX XXXX where the 3rd digit is regional. Numbers increase from south (0) to north (9).

Any phone numbers with other prefixes (02, 05, 08...) are even mobile numbers or from an old numbering plan which is still learnable but less logical than the current one.
